Space Radiation: NASA Protects Its Superheroes From Space Weather - Related Story: https://www.nasa.gov/feature/nasa-protects-its-super-heroes-from-space-weather
It’s not a bird or a plane but it might be a solar storm. We like to think of astronauts as our superheroes, but the reality is astronauts are not built like Superman who gains strength from the sun. In fact, much of the energy radiating from the sun is harmful to us mere mortals. Outside Earth’s protective magnetic field and atmosphere, the ionizing radiation in space will pose a serious risk to astronauts as they travel to Mars. High-energy galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) which are remnants from supernovas and solar storms like solar particle events (SPEs) and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) from the sun can cause harm to the body and spacecraft. These are all components of space weather.
When astronauts travel in space they can’t see or even feel radiation. However, NASA’s Human Research Program (HRP) is studying the effects radiation plays on the human body and developing ways to monitor and protect against this silent hazard. 
Learn how astronauts will endure space weather beyond low Earth orbit at https://www.nasa.gov/hrp/

NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Altered Immune System Responses. Core Mechanism: The stresses of spaceflight can awaken inactive viruses inside the bodies of astronauts, leading to rashes and other symptoms. Ongoing work seeks to further understand changes in the immune system to better protect astronaut health.

clinicalMetadata.risk_title: Risk of Altered Immune System Responses

knowledgeChunks.content: NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Altered Sensorimotor and Vestibular Function. Core Mechanism: Astronauts can experience motion sickness, issues with hand-eye or gait coordination, and dizziness during gravitational changes, making it difficult to walk or operate a vehicle. Ongoing research seeks to help astronauts recover faster from these changes so they can perform tasks inside and outside spacecraft.

clinicalMetadata.risk_title: Risk of Altered Sensorimotor and Vestibular Function

knowledgeChunks.content: NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations. Core Mechanism: Weightlessness alters blood circulation and how the heart and blood vessels function, potentially increasing the risk of cardiovascular events. Research focuses on minimizing these unhealthy changes.

NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Decompression Sickness. Core Mechanism: Transitioning from a pressurized spacecraft to a lower-pressure spacesuit can cause health and mission complications when dissolved nitrogen starts to bubble within body tissues. Research focuses on developing better prevention and faster treatment options.

NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Host-Microorganism Interactions. Core Mechanism: Skin and gut microbiomes can change in space, potentially increasing the risk of crew members getting sick. To help keep crews healthy, researchers are exploring these microbial ecosystems and how they evolve in space.

NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Hypoxia. Core Mechanism: Astronauts on future deep space missions will take steps to avoid “the bends” during spacewalks, but following those steps also elevates the risk of mild hypoxia — a condition that occurs when oxygen levels in body tissues become lower than normal.

NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Inadequate Food and Nutrition. Core Mechanism: A healthy, balanced diet is an essential element of crew health and performance. Ongoing research focuses on designing enjoyable, long-lasting, and nutritious meals for deep space missions and understanding the consequences of inadequate nutrition.

clinicalMetadata.risk_title: Risk of Inadequate Food and Nutrition

knowledgeChunks.content: NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Injury and Compromised Performance from Spacewalks. Core Mechanism: Working in a spacesuit is challenging. In addition to cognitive fatigue and injury, crew members must also manage risks in the spacewalk environment, including decompression sickness, and low oxygen and high carbon dioxide levels. Research focuses on characterizing human performance in spacesuits and balancing pressure and oxygen levels.

clinicalMetadata.risk_title: Risk of Injury and Compromised Performance from Spacewalks

knowledgeChunks.content: NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness. Core Mechanism: All astronauts perform exercise during their mission to counteract losses in bone density, muscle strength, and heart and blood vessel performance. Researchers are studying what types of exercise will best protect their health and their ability to perform spacewalks.

clinicalMetadata.risk_title: Risk of Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness

knowledgeChunks.content: NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS). Core Mechanism: The structure of the eyes and brain can change with spaceflight.  Research focuses on understanding the long-term health consequences of these changes and preventing them from occurring.

clinicalMetadata.risk_title: Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)

knowledgeChunks.content: NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Spaceflight-Induced Bone Changes. Core Mechanism: Without gravity, bones break down and become more brittle, boosting the chances of painful breaks. Ongoing research seeks to better understand and quantify these losses, and help preserve bone strength through diet, exercise, and medication.

NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders. Core Mechanism: Isolation, radiation, distance from Earth, and other intense space stressors may all take a toll on the mental health of the crew. Ongoing research seeks to better understand and quantify these psychological risks.

clinicalMetadata.risk_title: Risk of Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders

knowledgeChunks.content: NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Inadequate Teamwork. Core Mechanism: Selecting a crew that works well together is essential for mission success and safety. Researchers are studying how to help teams in prolonged isolation and confinement function efficiently and quickly recover after setbacks occur. They’re also mapping the myriad risks from miscommunications and related team tensions.

NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules. Core Mechanism: Space crews experience multiple hazards simultaneously. Stressors include chronic sleep loss, constant work demands, and irregularities in their internal biological clocks. Understanding how to reduce the effects of these stressors on crew health and safety is an ongoing area of research.

clinicalMetadata.risk_title: Risk of Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules

knowledgeChunks.content: NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Inadequate Systems Operations Support. Core Mechanism: Future crews on deep space missions must be able to live and work in an environment where they may face unexpected problems with software, vehicles, or other systems. Research focuses on understanding when crews need information, the types and timing of required training, or other support options.

clinicalMetadata.risk_title: Risk of Inadequate Systems Operations Support

knowledgeChunks.content: NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Injury from Dynamic Loads. Core Mechanism: During landing activities, crews risk getting injured. Understanding the likelihood of such injuries and how to better prevent them are areas of ongoing research.

clinicalMetadata.risk_title: Risk of Injury from Dynamic Loads

knowledgeChunks.content: NASA Human Research Program Official Risk: Risk of Radiation-Induced Cancers. Core Mechanism: Crews exposed to radiation from space may be more likely to develop cancer. Identifying the best ways to mitigate this risk and understand what interventions may help are ongoing research priorities.

NASA HRP Active Investigation: Immune Biomarkers (Immune Surveillance). Description: Scientists analyzed blood and saliva samples from Artemis II crew members to see how deep space changes the immune system.

knowledgeChunks.page: HRP Study: Artemis II Standard Measures
knowledgeChunks.content: NASA HRP Active Investigation: Artemis II Standard Measures (Deep Space Baseline). Description: Crews supplied a consistent set of health information to a data bank so that future researchers can learn more about astronaut health.

NASA HRP Active Investigation: B-Complex (SANS Metabolic Countermeasure). Description: Investigating if a daily B vitamin supplement can prevent or mitigate brain and eye changes that may affect some humans in space

NASA HRP Active Investigation: Brain Fluid Pressure (Intracranial ICP Dynamics). Description: Examining the relationship between fluid pressure inside the skull and changes to the eyes and brain of astronauts

NASA HRP Active Investigation: CIPHER (Integrated Human Multi-System Protocol). Description: Providing a better understand of how the human body changes while orbiting the Earth via a suite of studies examining multiple body systems

NASA HRP Active Investigation: Standard Measures (Physiological Setpoints). Description: Collecting a consistent set of physiological and psychological measurements to better understand how spaceflight affects the bodies and minds of crew members

NASA HRP Active Investigation: Thigh Cuff (Cephalad Venous Occlusion Countermeasure). Description: Testing if wearing tight thigh cuffs could keep more bodily fluids in the legs to help determine if future strategies can avert the eye disorders that can develop in space

NASA HRP Active Investigation: Venous Haemostasis (Thrombosis & Stasis Monitoring). Description: Examining physical differences in astronauts that may contribute to blood flow and blood coagulation changes in space

NASA HRP Active Investigation: Zero T2 (Compact Deep-Space Resistive Exercise). Description: Examining how exercise in space without a treadmill affects human health and performance ahead of deep space missions
NASA HRP Active Investigation: Altered Immunity (Cytokine & Viral Profiling). Description: Analyzing blood, saliva, and urine samples to investigate how spaceflight alters the immune system
NASA HRP Active Investigation: Food Acceptability (Nutritional Satiety). Description: Assessing how long-term spaceflight affects food appeal to improve current and future space food systems
NASA HRP Active Investigation: Food Physiology (Metabolic Optimization). Description: Determining whether an enhanced spaceflight diet could help astronauts better adapt to space

NASA HRP Active Investigation: Omics Archive (GeneLab Multi-Omics). Description: Collecting astronauts’ blood, urine, saliva, feces, and cells to document how long-duration spaceflight influences human health and performance and changes the body at the molecular level

NASA HRP Active Investigation: Space Gardening (Biophilic Psychological Countermeasure). Description: Surveying whether growing fresh vegetables in space can ease astronauts’ sense of isolation and confinement

NASA HRP Active Investigation: Spinal Health (Paraspinal Morphometry & Disc Protection). Description: Scrutinizing scans of astronauts’ spines to inform strategies that counter bone and muscle loss in space

NASA HRP Active Investigation: Tempus Pro (ExMC Autonomous Clinical Telemedicine). Description: Test-driving a commercial telemedicine device used to collect and integrate health data, potentially enabling remote, near real-time diagnoses

NASA HRP Active Investigation: Veggie Monitoring (HRP Clinical Investigation). Description: Monitoring microbial growth on hardware that stores crops in space to develop a better plant production system and ensure crew safety

Canadian Space Agency (CSA) CANS (Canadian Active Neutron Spectrometer) Operational Mission: Compact, autonomous instrument developed with Bubble Technology Industries to measure high-risk neutron radiation exposure in deep space missions to the Moon and Mars.

thresholds: ~30% total ISS radiation is secondary neutrons

knowledgeChunks.content: Secondary Neutron Radiotoxicity in Spaceflight: Neutron radiation contributes to approximately 30% of total astronaut radiation dose inside space habitats. High-energy GCR particles collide with spacecraft aluminum shielding, creating high-LET secondary neutron cascades that cause severe biological tissue damage and double-strand DNA breaks requiring continuous autonomous monitoring.

Canadian Active Neutron Spectrometer (CANS) Autonomous Capabilities: Successor to Canadian bubble detectors, MOSFET, EVARM, and Radi-N/Radi-N2 experiments. Unlike passive bubble detectors requiring manual post-EVA bubble counting, CANS operates continuously and autonomously on spacecraft hulls, streaming real-time neutron energy spectra into astronaut clinical monitoring systems.

CSA Accelerated Aging Model of Microgravity: Weightlessness changes the human body in ways directly analogous to accelerated physiological aging and extreme sedentary decubitus. Spaceflight accelerates arterial stiffening, insulin resistance, bone mineral density loss (osteopenia), and vestibular balance impairment, providing a compressed clinical model for terrestrial degenerative disease.

Deep-Space Exploration Multi-Stress Risk Matrix: Moon and Mars transit profiles induce compounded hazards: (1) prolonged microgravity, (2) elevated unshielded galactic cosmic ray/neutron exposure, (3) extreme isolation and psychological confinement, (4) two-way communication latency (5 to 22 minutes each way), and (5) total inability to evacuate or receive Earth medical resupply, mandating fully autonomous edge AI medical monitoring.

Canadian ISS Multi-Organ Physiological Investigations: Target organ systems scrutinized by CSA clinical studies include: (1) Bones (trabecular demineralization and osteoporotic microarchitecture loss), (2) Cardiovascular (arterial wall remodeling, endothelial vascular stiffness), and (3) Brain and Vestibular (post-flight balance recovery and neuro-vestibular reweighting).
